Tulsa, Oklahoma (October 11, 2018) <U+2013> On June 28, 2018 our Oklahoma Supreme Court voted that the Oklahoma Tax Commission was wrong to deny rebates to CompSource Mutual Insurance Co. and the Oklahoma Association of Electric Self Insurers for money assessed on behalf of the Multiple Injury Trust Fund. The rebates amount to an accrued debt backlog of nearly $200 million because of poorly written laws. This decision, associated government malfunction, and long-term consequences underscore some important issues facing voters in the coming November 6 elections. It has become obvious, if it wasn<U+2019>t already, that the Oklahoma Legislature, including Glen Mulready and Leslie Osborn, and Governor Fallin have failed their duty to taxpayers to fix the laws that obligate Oklahoma taxpayers to pay out $100 million in 2018 on top of the roughly $90 million in previously paid rebates. Gov. Mary Fallin and a legislative leader said lawmakers believed they had ended the rebates when they rewrote the state workers<U+2019> compensation laws in 2011 and again in 2013; however, <U+201C>the language intended to eliminate the rebates was either left out or not written clearly enough to ensure that it happened,<U+201D> Fallin said, in a written order. Our speculation is, that if state legislators had ever read or written the laws to begin with, they would have known of the errors in the laws. The Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled, due to the way the laws still read, the Oklahoma Tax Commission was wrong to deny rebates to CompSource Mutual Insurance Co. and the Oklahoma Association of Electric Self Insurers for money assessed on behalf of Multiple Injury Trust Fund. The Tax Commission originally denied those requests, saying the statutory authority for the rebates had been repealed by an executive order from Gov. Mary Fallin in 2015. However, the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled in June that the rebates authorized by the Legislature had not been repealed. "The two orders of the Tax Commission are reversed, and the proceedings are remanded to the Tax Commission for the appropriate processing," Justice James Edmondson wrote in the decision. CompSource and the Oklahoma Association of Electric Self Insurers Fund were denied payment of interest on their rebates. <U+201C>The legal team for the Oklahoma Tax Commission is reviewing the decision and meeting with the Tax Commissioner to determine a course of action and whether other companies will be owed rebates in the wake of the decision,<U+201D> Tax Commission Spokeswoman, Paula Ross, said Thursday. Local attorney Bob Burke estimates the decision could mean the backlog of rebates could cost the state tens of millions more. Insurers and self-insured companies are assessed for Multiple Injury Trust Fund, which provides benefits for workers that suffer permanent total disability due to multiple workplace accidents. The money is paid to the Tax Commission, which deposits it into the Workers<U+2019> Compensation Assessment Rebate Fund. If we called the Workers<U+2019> Compensation Assessment Rebate Fund what it really is, it would just be called the Insurance Company<U+2019>s Money for Not Paying Injured Workers Piggy Bank. Traditionally, under state law, insurers have been allowed to request a rebate for two-thirds of their assessment. The Oklahoma Supreme Court<U+2019>s June 28 decision highlights the lack of confidence voters should have in electing current legislators to important state agencies, especially when their voting record and bill sponsorship makes them directly accountable for harming working Oklahomans and Taxpayers. The multi-year legislative debacle of rewriting the unconstitutional Oklahoma Worker<U+2019>s Compensation code, multiple times, cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars in insurance company rebates being paid out while injured workers are paid pennies, if at all, for injuries that cause lifelong disabilities. Said the candidates, <U+201C>You don<U+2019>t reassign chairs on the Titanic and think Oklahoma<U+2019>s ship won<U+2019>t still sink.<U+201D> Mulready and Osborn owe taxpayers and Oklahoma workers the truth on their votes, bill sponsorship and rhetoric leading to the latest ruling from the Oklahoma Supreme Court that created a new obligation of one hundred million dollars in rebate assessment due to insurers. They, along with Mary Fallin, need to explain this failure of leadership and negligence of duty to Oklahoma residents.

The heat index was 103. All two thermostats were at 65 degrees and for the moment the room was cool. The attendees were coming in and the one page program was handed out, one to a family. As all were seated we brought the casket down the center isle and the director asked all to stand. The family followed the casket in and behind them came the preacher. He was dressed in his best suit, his only suit, which he had worn to his wedding 17 years before. The button at the neck was missing and the tie was knotted seven inches below his Adams apple. A yellowed T-shirt was prominent. The rolls of adipose tissue bulged under his arms and were wrapped tight by the coat he had overpowered several years ago. I knew him well and I knew he was relishing what he would say. He began. "I stand before you today to deliver a message that is on my heart. I have prayed about this since hearing of the deceased's passing. I knew him well." The newly widowed was in the front row with family. Appearing at least 70 she was in her early 50's. Puffy, balding and expressionless. The first two rows on the preacher's left were children, grandchildren and great grandchildren. The chapel was full but most did not know the deceased or the family. The only air conditioned building on the mountain was a huge draw and there were refreshments following the burial. An unusually large crowd was present as it was an away weekend for both Alabama and Auburn. "With a heavy heart" the preacher started "the ultimate forgiveness is the Lord's, but we all know there is no way this man lying in this box before me can enter the gates of heaven. If there was evil to be done he did it twice. He was just no good" The scream from the widow as she slid to the floor, paralyzed all present and several relatives had to be restrained. One came over several pews lurching toward the preacher while foaming out words in strange tongues. Trying to regain control the Pastor defended his remarks by saying he was led by God and that he was following the teachings of Jesus, and that if anyone would like to say a few words about the dead they may do so. Three rows from the back a man stood and said "His brother was worse" At the cemetery the preacher was given a good beating. Speaking truth to power can have it's downside. PG

Restore Net Neutrality: A long and storied strain of populism runs through the history of our great state. Oklahomans have always had an independent streak and since statehood, we've been able to transcend partisan politics and understand some economic issues as just plain old common sense. Today, the people of Oklahoma understand that a free and open internet is critical to our ability to connect with loved ones and to have our voices heard, not to mention our ability to thrive in a competitive 21st-century economy. National polling has consistently shown that the vast majority of voters <U+2014> 82 percent of Republicans, 90 percent of Democrats and 85 percent of independents <U+2014> oppose the Federal Communications Commission's recent repeal of net neutrality protections. So, why aren't the people's representatives in Washington, D.C., doing anything about it? And more specifically, why haven't Reps. Tom Cole, Steve Russell and our other members of Congress followed the bipartisan lead of the Senate in advancing a Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolution that would restore net neutrality? You don't have to read public polling numbers to know that net neutrality is a nonpartisan issue. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said it best when he voted in May for the CRA overturning the repeal of net neutrality rules: <U+201C>You either trust your cable company or you don't. If you trust your cable company, you won't like my vote. If you don't trust your cable company, you will like my vote.<U+201D> Ask your friends, family, neighbors and coworkers if they trust <U+2014> or even like <U+2014> their cable and internet providers. I think you know what you'll hear. That's really what net neutrality boils down to <U+2014> it's a question of whether we trust the companies that bring internet into our homes and businesses not to make a pretty penny by discriminating against certain types of online content. These companies already make a solid profit by charging us for access to the web. Without net neutrality, they'll be able to monetize the other side of the web <U+2014> charging businesses and organizations to access their client base. Those who can afford it will end up with faster, prioritized access. Those who can't will end up in the slow lane. You better believe Silicon Valley companies will get priority access and Oklahoma's small businesses will be left in the dust. When our representatives return to Washington in September, they have a decision to make and it's summed up nicely in Sen. Kennedy's quote: Will they side with ridiculously rich cable and internet companies trying to lobby for a new revenue stream? Or will they side with everyday Oklahomans, small-business owners, community organizations and local media companies who want a free and open internet? I encourage our members of Congress to reach down into that deep well of populism in our state's history and side with the people by supporting the net neutrality CRA. TOLLS ARE JUST ANOTHER TAX (NO TOLLS!) (An Op-Ed by State Representative Craig Fishbein) There<U+2019>s a saying at the Capitol that no legislation is truly dead until midnight on the final day of session <U+2013> when state law requires the legislature to stop working, and resets the calendar to zero in anticipation of the next session. This year, as is every year, many ideas were left to wither and die on the vine for a myriad of reasons that range from political to fiscal. Thankfully, one proposal that died as the clock ran out, was to institute tolls on Connecticut highways. There were a few different bills, but the underlying theme of all was to install tolls all over the state, and tax drivers for (egads!) daring to travel to and from their work, their appointments, their shopping, or merely to visit friends or family who happen to live a few towns away. These were also made under the guise of bringing in revenue to repair Connecticut<U+2019>s crumbling roads and bridges. Now, some may argue a toll isn<U+2019>t a <U+201C>tax.<U+201D> I wholeheartedly disagree; a toll is absolutely a tax. Drivers who use toll roads are paying an extra penalty <U+2013> a tax <U+2013> on top of the enormous taxes they<U+2019>re already paying on gas, licenses and permits, and the property tax for merely owning a vehicle in the first place. Advertisement Proposals show as many as 80 toll gantries on nearly all of Connecticut<U+2019>s major roadways, including Interstates 91, 95, 84, 395, 691 and Routes 15, 8, 2, and more. Toll fees would (presently) range between 3.5 cents per mile to 11.8 cents per mile. Therefore, an ordinary commuter trip between Hartford and New Haven would cost about $800 or more annually. But even that estimate is controlled by the price charged by the tolling system, which is hard to know because they are also proposing a congestion pricing toll system. Congestion price tolling is where the toll prices raise or decline based upon the amount of vehicles on the roadway. Congestion pricing could mean an extra 25% more per mile for driving during designated <U+201C>rush hour<U+201D> times. Of course, taking into account that rush hour will be when most of Connecticut<U+2019>s residents must get to and from work that means about 70% of all toll revenue collected will come from Connecticut residents. Some say, how about just border tolls? No can do. When Connecticut agreed to remove its tolls in 1983, it was authorized to charge one of the highest gas taxes in the nation, and to receive a greater portion of federal transportation dollars. The installation of border tolls now would jeopardize $100s of Millions is past and future federal funds. Toll proponents<U+2019> claim a <U+201C>lock box<U+201D> will be set up to ensure collected funds will be used for the proper purposes. History shows that a <U+201C>lock box<U+201D> is only as good as the lock that secures it. If everyone has a key, there<U+2019>s no telling how long it will remain filled. In 1983, the current Special Transportation Fund was set up as a dedicated fund to finance the state<U+2019>s transportation infrastructure program and operate the DOT and DMV. By 1987, the fund was being used for non-transportation purposes. Plus, any revenue gained from enacting and erecting tolls will be years away, have no impact on the state<U+2019>s current fiscal crisis and will undoubtedly add more state bureaucracy and the associated salaries and pension costs that come with that expansion of government Tolls are also a bad idea because people will naturally try to avoid them, putting greater stress on local roadways, leading to greater local congestion, and resulting in municipal tax increases Just over a month ago, even though the legislature did not authorize tolls during session, nor did it appropriate any monies for the same, the Governor convened the 10 member State Bonding Commission (which he Chairs) for the purposes of borrowing $10 Million for another study of tolls. (FYI, there have been at least three such studies already completed within recent years.) Shortly thereafter, I joined my House Republican colleagues in signing a petition to go into special session to try and stop the borrowing. Unfortunately though, the House Democrats refused to sign the petition, a special session was not authorized, and the Governor<U+2019>s continued reckless borrowing goes on, unchallenged. Thankfully in 2018, tolls succumbed to the stroke of midnight. Unfortunately though, I<U+2019>m confident they<U+2019>ll be resurrected as early as January, 2019. As a very famous Yankee once said, <U+201C>It ain<U+2019>t over till it<U+2019>s over.<U+201D>

Earlier this week, I had the opportunity to speak in front of a group of high school students and staff. During this time, a comment was made about making higher education tuition free, and because this was part of a larger question, I did not directly address this specific point. I believe that we should make all personal education expenses tax deducible at the State level, but making college tuition free is something that both cannot be done, nor should it be done. If you ever thought that getting a new drivers license at your local Secretary of State was hassle, consider the following... The US Census Bureau estimates that Michigan has a population of nearly 10 million, with nearly 7.8 million being 18 or older. Given the personnel and physical size constraints of our public universities, providing free courses to over 7.8 million residents would crash the system, requiring some other way to limit enrollment. If they only offered classes on a first come first serve basis, then it would take even longer to complete a degree program because nearly every class would be over-filled on the first day of enrollment. Without a cost factor, how would they limit "student" population in an effective manner to ensure a timely completion for given programs? Age? Gender identity? Social status? Relations or referrals? Lottery? Geographic proximity (so much for online learning)? Test scores and grades only? No matter what, there has to be some limiting conditions, as such, having financial price to pay for educational services is the most effect, and most honorable, way to limit access to higher education. However, attending a college is not the only way to receive an education, and with modern technology, and the free market, an instructor does not need to be in the same state as their students. Yet, at any stage of education, the student is solely responsible for learning. Parents, teachers, coaches, professor's aides, and others can offer assistance, but in the end, the student is the one who must put in the effort of learning the material. (This is a lesson that I personally learned the hard way.) Therefore, by making education expenses, including student loan payments, tax free, Michigan can provide an incentive for everyone to seek out education in a manner they desire, without flooding campuses across the state.

Note: I put this post up back in September of last year, and of course with the chronic bad Salem leadership, chronic problems have persisted, and so I am putting it up again today, almost one year later. The wildfires continue to rage and the solutions remain the same, but no one is doing anything...except Donald Trump and his crew back in DC, Greg Walden, and of course our heroic crews on the fire lines (and we already know fire-fighting on the ground is possibly the most dangerous and debilitating work there is anywhere). I see nothing more than "ain't it awful" platitudes from Kate Brown, Knute Buehler, and the legislature, as Rural Oregon continues to suffer. To bring this piece up to date, I've made a few tweaks, but the message hasn't changed: How many communities in the state of Oregon have under 5,000 in population? Two hundred and seventy five. You know it and I know it: economically and socially, heartbreakingly, almost all of these rural communities are shells of what they were before over-zealous (yes, radical) environmentalism in the early 80<U+2019>s shut down surrounding forests; before progressivism took charge in Salem; before jobs, wood products and county timber receipts vanished. And since then <U+2013> add insult to injury <U+2013> these forests have been ignored by their federal and state masters<U+2026>and so they are burning. The USFS expends more than half of its annual budget combating wildfires but nonetheless, three years ago in an especially tough fire season, fire destroyed 4% of our total Oregon forests, the huge percentage of it on public land. As I write this in mid-August 2018 we<U+2019>ve lost almost another 3%. (2017? Not quite so bad, but horrible nonetheless, especially for incredible air pollution across the state. The Oregon forest is our garden. And like any garden, it must be cultivated and not left to go fallow<U+2026>and then to catch fire. After long decades of little thinning and logging and plenty of fire-exclusion, we have tens of millions of acres of forest with too-thick stands that are smothering in themselves. They are diseased and dying: too many trees per acre. Excessive fuel on the ground and in standing dead trees. It<U+2019>s a tinderbox. One lightning strike and there is Hell-to-pay. The tragedy is not that the wildfires get started in the first place (in the Northwest, most are due to lightning strikes). The tragedy is that once they<U+2019>ve started, they instantly get blow-torch hot and can<U+2019>t be stopped. Unlike hurricanes, the huge majority of the current out-of-control wildfires could have been altogether prevented, or extinguished in their early stages. Oddly enough, nature used to handle the excessive-fuel problem with frequent lightning-generated low-intensity, relatively cool understory surface fires, often set purposely by native Indian populations: this was active management! Now, it<U+2019>s too late for the prescribed-burn solution for the millions of acres that must be treated. There<U+2019>s just too much forest, too much fuel, and the seasonal window for this proptocol is too short. Today, the bulk of the problem must be handled mechanically: road construction crews creating access, chainsaw teams, timber harvester and articulated skidders in the east regions, and in the coast range, high-lead and skyline logging. This decades-long lack of active forest cultivation has been a massive mechanical error-of-omission by the USFS and the BLM <U+2013> and to a lesser degree, the State of Oregon <U+2013> held hostage by an un-informed urban society and their inept political leaders. Most definitely, this is a top-level management problem. Our professional foresters know what preventative measures should be taken, they<U+2019>re just unable to make them happen. It<U+2019>s not their fault. To be clear, these fires are not occurring because of <U+201C>global climate change,<U+201D> as Governor Kate Brown has off-handedly declared. That<U+2019>s absurd, and it<U+2019>s no wonder that in this time of catastrophe she only offers tepid applause to our firefighters, along with the occasional <U+201C>be careful out there<U+201D> tutelage to the rest of us. She says, <U+201C>it<U+2019>s bad out there,<U+201D> while offering no plan for how this horror can be prevented next year or the year after. For our current political leadership it<U+2019>s about fire-killing, not fire prevention. The progressive far-left strategy is to not take mechanical fire prevention measures, but to leave a forest alone; not to tend to it, not to prune it, not to take a chainsaw into a wilderness area to douse a smoldering lightning-struck snag; not to harvest the millions of board feet of still-usable timber that remains after a major burn (e.g. southern Oregon's Kalmiopsis Wilderness has burned three times in 30 years). And certainly, our leftist leaders are loath to harvest any of our forests. Logging, they say, is so<U+2026>Neanderthal. But these same leaders are more than willing to expend enormous amounts of taxpayer money attempting to quell the fires that are a direct result of their own negligence. So we have massive wildfires and sullen small-town poverty. Over a period of four decades, millions of Oregonians have been left to exist without economic opportunity <U+2013> a quiet social disaster that their DC and Salem overseers ignore. Pretty much everyone agrees that excess-fuel is the cause of the problem. Even our wack-a-doddle progressive Democrat U.S. Senator Ron Wyden hit the right note two years ago in a presentation to the Senate: <U+201C>The idea of ripping off prevention, which you need most, defies common sense<U+2026>shoddy budgeting today leads to bigger fires tomorrow.<U+201D> And suppression is expensive. John Bailey, Professor of Silviculture and Fire Management at Oregon State University in Corvallis, said, <U+201C>It<U+2019>s bankrupting us. The irony is we steal from the positive things we can do in order to keep suppressing forest fires, even though suppression makes next year<U+2019>s fire season worse.<U+201D> And back to global climate change: if that is even a small part of the problem, why isn<U+2019>t Kate Brown calling for the Forest Service, State Forestry, and the BLM to clean things up to reduce the fire danger? And yes, the USFS and BLM oversee federal land, but a governor has enormous influence. Governors from the Western states can present a united effort to demand that either the federal government manage the land appropriately, or turn it back to our states. It<U+2019>s pure and simple, and it<U+2019>s my bet the Trump Administration will give an immediate blessing to the former and would be sympathetic to the latter. Kate Brown should provide that coordination and leadership. Would Knute Buehler do what is necessary to coordinate with the feds should he become governor? What do you think, based on his personal attacks on the President? And what about logging? Referring to the approximately 20,000,000 acres of Oregon public land forests, the Oregon Department of Forestry says, <U+201C>public lands are now harvesting approximately 11 percent of public forest<U+2019>s potential for growing timber.<U+201D> In contrast, of the 10,000,000 acres of private forests in Oregon, the Department lists the potential-for-growing-timber statistic at 93%. It<U+2019>s OK to cut down trees! Timber and smaller-dimension wood products are the ultimate sustainable natural resource. Let<U+2019>s judiciously use what God has given us. Let<U+2019>s tend the garden! What do European government forestlands and southeastern U.S. private forestlands have in common? They<U+2019>re intensively managed, with clean understory, regular thinning, prescribed fire (controlled burning), sustainable timber harvesting, lots of forest-jobs<U+2026>and hardly ever a wildfire. And no small thing, and unlike so much of our U.S. government lands, these forests tend to be open to the surrounding populations. So, in a massive, CCC-like system improvement project <U+2013> using Federal money to contract out to local private firms <U+2013> let<U+2019>s insist our leadership overseas preventative maintenance on our millions of acres of neglected USFS/BLM-controlled Oregon forest, including the employment of hundreds of teams of young people from our economically stricken rural communities. Let<U+2019>s put them out there in the woods <U+2013> yes with chain saws <U+2013> tending to our forests so they can become healthy again by doing very simple mechanical cultivation tasks: tree thinning, cleanup, prescribed burning, and harvesting. Our Oregon woodlands <U+2013> this neglected garden of overgrown, diseased, and stunted trees <U+2013> will breathe again as we stimulate the entire Oregon economy by bringing wood products to the market. The wildfires? When they start, they will be quickly quelled. And especially <U+2013> and this is personal for me because I was born and raised in a small impoverished back-country town <U+2013> there will be jobs, jobs, jobs for the good people who live in these rural regions. There would be no losers in this effort. This really IS a management problem, one that has everything to do with Salem leadership<U+2019>s inability to take mechanical action. We need an Oregon Red Trifecta. (A Red Trifecta is when the governor<U+2019>s seat and both sides of the legislative branch are held by the same political party). Until then, we might as well accept wildfire devastation as the new-normal. -sam #MOGA #orpol #orgov #DirtyPolitics #DrainTheSwamp

Dr. Cedric Hayden and I said when we brought Measure 101 to the ballot that our Medicaid system was failing. We said it needed a full reset. Then FamilyCare was forced out of the market over a reimbursement rate dispute and for political reasons. Their patients went to CareOregon. Now CareOregon is upside down $100 MILLION. And the state needs another $830 MILLION next year to fill a new two-year shortfall for Medicaid. Friends, we have been raising the red flag on this for several years. We felt it was so important that we took the ponzi-like tax scheme passed by the legislature to the ballot to try to stop healthcare dollars from being swept away from Medicaid and to let voters know what was really happening in our healthcare system. Then the legislature spent those M101 dollars on things unrelated to healthcare, and Governor Brown gave CCOs windfall bonuses that don't have to be spent on healthcare. One bonus, $20 million, is going back to FamilyCare and they no longer serve patients! The solution to this matter was always in the original Medicaid bill from 2011 that I supported - put public employees in the CCOs, balance out the risk pool, and level off the healthcare expenditures for Medicaid and public employee plans. In doing so, we'd have the money to cover both low-income Oregonians and public employee plans. Two governors have failed to implement the original law, and here we are with a system that is breaking right in front of our eyes. Unchecked, it will bankrupt the state or result in cutting care to people in need. Taxing other people's healthcare was never a way to solve this issue. In 2019, I'm going to redraft the two options that will save the Medicaid program - move public employees into the exchange so savings can be redirected to Medicaid, or put public employees into CCOs. Either bill is the only way we can resolve this issue if we're going to keep serving low-income Oregonians who need healthcare. $100 MILLION dollars in new losses is totally unsustainable. #FixMediciad #healthcarereform #orleg https://www.oregonlive.com/business/index.ssf/2018/08/post_267.html

I would like to stress to you that all Oklahomans that need help, if they do not make enough in their wages to meet basic critical needs like FOOD, SHELTER AND HEALTH CARE, receive tax dollars through state programs. People question why we have stagnant wages so how is putting an unnecessary burden on taxpayers to support sub par wages to protect poor business models okay to continue? Oklahoma's current minimum wage is $7.25 per hour, the same as federal minimum wage. Oklahoma's minimum wage applies to any employer that grosses $100,000 or more a year, OR hires ten or more employees. Oklahoma does not have a unique minimum wage, and instead adopts the Federal Minimum Wage by reference. Oklahoma sets a special minimum wage of $2.00 per hour for work not covered by the Federal Minimum Wage, including full time students. Any employees under the age of 22 who are enrolled as full-time students are exempt from Oklahoma's minimum wage law (but the special minimum wage of $2.00 per hour still applies). Additional exempt employees include farm and ranch workers, maids, government employees, railroad workers, temporary part-time employees, feed store employees, and deputy sheriffs. Exempt means they are unprotected because they are not required to be paid the minimum wage. Additional minimum wage statutes allow Oklahoma employers to deduct the cost of uniforms from their employee's wages. If employers fail to pay the legal minimum wage to an employee, they could be liable to pay up to double the amount of wages owed to the employee. Oklahoma employers may not pay you under $7.25 per hour unless you or your occupation are specifically exempt from the minimum wage under state or federal law. Again, the burden of a business that only prospers by sacrificing the well being of its employees should not be placed upon the shoulders of Oklahoma wage earners.

The News Record started their Q&A last week. Lets look at the first question-one regarding education funding. My answer follows, along with additional comments that were left out of the paper version due to word count restrictions. I always try to educate in my answers so that my constituents get the same information that I do. If you have further questions, leave them in the comments section and I'll address them there. Q: The Wyoming state constitution guarantees education as a governmental service for Wyoming residents. And education also is the state<U+2019>s top priority for spending and support. What does that specifically mean to you as legislators continue to grapple with funding issues in K-12 education? A: One of the most important duties of the legislature is providing an effective and excellent public education at every school for every student. Without a doubt, we can<U+2019>t be a great state without great schools. Both the legislature and local school boards make funding decisions. The legislature sends a block grant of money to local districts based on a complicated state model. The local school board then makes all decisions on how to spend that block grant. This includes decisions about administrators, personnel, salaries, insurance, supplies, technology, activities, classes, curriculum, transportation, etc. The legislature doesn't make decisions about sports, band, or which classes schools must offer (outside of the legislated mandatory subject areas), nor should it. I'm in favor of our local school board members making these local decisions. According to state data, Campbell County had an average daily membership (ADM) of 8,577 students and an annual budget of $137,792,053 (not including reserves--about $20.1 million), averaging $16,065 per student last school year. Our district employed 1,606 employees: 641 being teachers and 51 being administrators for our district's 23 schools. Last year<U+2019>s cuts reduced our district<U+2019>s budget to $136,612,000. That said, the 2018/2019 guarantee from the state is still projected to grow to $138,120,000. I did not vote for last years cuts. In part because of the cuts made the previous year on top of our reduces ADM, and also in part because last year's cuts were made to the most vulnerable in special education. I understand the need to balance our expenditures with our income. It just doesn't make sense to me that we would target our most vulnerable student population first. I don't agree with that, and I couldn't vote for that. We are projected to be several hundreds of millions short state wide in future school years. The good news is that we have a large rainy day fund ($1.6 billion) to serve as a buffer. I don<U+2019>t believe drastic cuts or taxes are needed now, but some action is needed. I believe we need to do the following immediately: 1. Slow the growth of rising costs and gov<U+2019>t creep. This includes addressing the rising costs of health insurance, something we are actively pursuing on the Labor/Health committee which I'm on. 2. Open the books and see if we<U+2019>re being as efficient as possible with taxpayer dollars. Last year, an organization called Open the Books uncovered $10 million in credit card expenses in Natrona County<U+2019>s district. About $1.2 million alone was spent on travel and entertainment, and <U+201C>household<U+201D> items totaled $1.37 million. This is not good. The charges were downright embarrassing for our state and raises the question of efficient spending, and that is just one county. I<U+2019>m committed to making learning more efficient, effective, and accountable. By now most of us have seen the AFP mailers, which are trying to get you to vote Republican because of high property taxes. Let's take a look at this shall we? First of all, this is Johnson County. The median home value is nearly a quarter of a million dollars (https://smartasset.com/taxes/kansas-property-tax-calculator). Given the demand for homes due to a stabilizing real estate economy since the recession of 2008, your property value has only been increasing (https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article200633529.html). This is part of the reason why your property taxes have gone up. However, Johnson County actually has the 9th-lowest effective property tax rate in the state of Kansas, currently sitting it 1.28%. Yes, we do pay the highest property taxes in the state in terms of dollar amount, but the rate is much lower than the majority of counties in Kansas. Next, lets talk about education. Blue Valley schools are so good because a decent chunk of change from your property taxes goes towards funding them. This does go towards education funding in general for Kansas as well. So why can't other parts of Kansas afford it themselves? Let's look at tax cuts. Your property taxes had actually been decreasing or stable between 2007-2013 (http://www.kansasopengov.org/kog/databank#report_id=38&county=Johnson). It was only after the worst of the Brownback income tax cuts had begun to take effect that your property taxes went up. Why did this happen? Because revenue has to come from somewhere. The sales tax on food was only just implemented in 2013. These regressive taxes have hurt lower class and working class families in Kansas the most, because a 7.5%-10% tax on food won't be noticed by someone making a high 6-figure or 7-figure salary, but it will be noticed by a family of five trying to survive on $65k a year. In essence, those making less are actually paying a higher effective tax rate. Bottom line, taxes are complicated, and anyone who tries to tell you that they are a simple solution to job growth, wage growth and puts more money in your pocket is flat out lying. The tax cuts did not encourage businesses to come here, and it didn't encourage job growth, because guess what? When someone is given a tax cut, they keep those savings. Corporations don't use tax savings to create jobs, they use it in stock buybacks and raises for their executives. Tax cuts mean budget cuts, and funds for education and healthcare always seem to be the first to get the ax. If you've stuck with me this long, I really appreciate it. We need fiscal responsibility in Kansas. We need representatives who won't lie to you just so their pockets and the pockets of their biggest donors get fatter. Remember this: Kansas has had a Republican governor for eight years. Republicans outnumber Democrats in the state legislature and in the state senate by a near 3 to 1 margin. So if you're looking for someone to blame for budget shortfalls, decreased revenue, and higher property taxes, you don't have to look far. This year, vote for someone who at least has different ideas. Vote for someone who is going to think about what's best for all of Kansas, and not just the Koch brothers and their friends.

I<U+2019>m pleased to announce that the Massachusetts State Senate recently passed legislation to protect individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities from caregivers found to have substantiated charges of abuse. The legislation is known to many as Dana<U+2019>s Law or Nicky<U+2019>s Law. This is a bill that I have been working on since I was sworn into office after I met Dana<U+2019>s parents. In our first meeting they told me about how their son, Dana, had been mentally and physically abused by his caretakers. Surprisingly, after that caretaker was fired, she then turned around and applied for a job at a new facility and would have been hired had Dana<U+2019>s mother not worked at the same facility. The bill establishes a registry for caretakers found to have committed abuse against individuals with intellectual or developmental disabilities. Employers serving these populations would be required to screen potential employees during the application process, so that any individual who appears on the registry will not be hired. The legislation also allows the Disabled Persons Protection Commission to take action against an employer who fails to check the registry or who utilizes the services of a caretaker whose name appears on the registry by imposing a monetary fine of up to $5,000, revoking or downgrading a license, forfeiting a state contract, or a combination of these penalties. What happened to Dana and Nicky should never happen again and we must do everything in our power to ensure those who take care of disabled persons are compassionate, respectful, and kind.

The state's school administrative reorganization law passed in June 2007 requires school districts to consolidate administrative services. Plans and budgets for new regional school units must be approved by participating communities. Terry Driscoll, a selectman and member of the school district Reorganization Planning Committee; Bill Reinhardt, a SAD 50 representative and member of the committee; and Town Manager John Falla, an at-large member of the committee, spent more than an hour explaining the ins and outs of the new law Thursday. The Maine Department of Education had approved the committee's consolidation plan for a new regional school unit earlier that day. The committee that worked on the consolidation effort is composed of three representatives of each of the six towns in the two districts: Rockland, Owls Head and South Thomaston of SAD 5, and Cushing, Thomaston and St. George of SAD 50. As proposed, the school board for the new regional school unit would have 13 members serving staggered three-year terms. Rockland would have five members; Thomaston, three; St. George, two; and Owls Head, South Thomaston, and Cushing, one each. Driscoll said the people have to consider the pace of valuation growth in the communities.
